query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In steels designed for chemical-processing and nuclear applications, the controlled addition of a minor amount of aluminum enhances corrosion resistance by forming a chromium‐rich passive layer that is maintained through a sacrificial redox buffering mechanism. Specifically, the preferential oxidation (or dissolution) of aluminum creates a protective Al/AlCl3 redox couple that slows the depletion of chromium from the alloy, thereby stabilizing the passivation film under corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A duplex stainless steel (e.g., DS2205) or similar high-performance steel with standard chromium content and microstructure produced by conventional processing methods.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low concentration of aluminum into the steel’s alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Expose the modified steels and a baseline (aluminum-free) counterpart to aggressive chemical processing environments (e.g., aqueous chloride solutions or molten salt conditions) at elevated temperatures, representative of nuclear reactor or chemical plant settings.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and maintenance of a continuous, chromium-rich passive film at the steel surface, assisted by the formation of protective aluminum oxide or chloride species.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum acts as a sacrificial element that undergoes preferential oxidation/dissolution. This process forms a redox couple (Al/AlCl3 in chloride environments) that buffers the local electrochemical potential, thereby reducing the rate at which chromium is dissolved from the steel. The preserved chromium content in the passive layer ensures sustained protection against corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with the aluminum addition will exhibit significantly reduced chromium depletion (thinner or non-propagating depletion zones) and lower overall corrosion rates compared to the baseline steel without aluminum when measured under identical testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Steel with an identical composition and processing history except for the absence of the additional aluminum.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in corrosive environments typical of chemical processing (e.g., high chloride concentrations) and molten salt conditions at elevated temperatures. The hypothesis applies primarily to steels where chromium is the main passivating element and the aluminum concentration is optimized to avoid deleterious effects on other mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of the protective effect may depend on other alloying elements, microstructural features, and the exact corrosive environment conditions. The interplay between aluminum’s sacrificial role and other diffusion-driven enhancements (e.g., from grain boundary diffusion in ultra-fine-grained steels) needs further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples with identical processing histories – one set with a controlled addition of aluminum and one set serving as the baseline without aluminum. Expose both sets to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt at a fixed elevated temperature) for a predetermined period. Use surface analytical techniques, such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), to quantify chromium depletion depth and assess the integrity of the passive film.
measurements: Surface composition profiling (especially chromium and aluminum content) via XPS.
Corrosion rate measurements using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization tests.
Microstructural characterization of corrosion attack regions via SEM/EDX.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-containing steel does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both chromium depletion depth and corrosion rate compared to the baseline steel under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that a sacrificial redox buffering mechanism provided by aluminum enhances corrosion resistance will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
